{{short description|Geometric relation between a triangle's side lengths and cevian length}}
In [[geometry]], '''Stewart's theorem''' yields a relation between the lengths of the sides and the length of a [[cevian]] in a triangle. Its name is in honour of the Scottish mathematician [[Matthew Stewart (mathematician)|Matthew Stewart]], who published the theorem in 1746.<ref>{{citation|first=Matthew|last=Stewart|title=Some General Theorems of Considerable Use in the Higher Parts of Mathematics|year=1746|publisher=Sands, Murray and Cochran|place=Edinburgh}} "Proposition II"</ref>

== Statement ==
[[File:Stewarts theorem.svg|thumb|Diagram of Stewart's theorem]]

Let {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}} be the lengths of the sides of a triangle.  Let {{mvar|d}} be the length of a [[cevian]] to the side of length {{mvar|a}}.  If the cevian divides the side of length {{mvar|a}} into two segments of length {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|n}}, with {{mvar|m}} adjacent to {{mvar|c}} and {{mvar|n}} adjacent to {{mvar|b}}, then Stewart's theorem states that
<math display="block">b^2m + c^2n = a(d^2 + mn).</math>

A common [[mnemonic]] used by students to memorize this equation (after rearranging the terms) is:
<math display="block">\underset{\text{A }man\text{ and his }dad}{man\ +\ dad} = \!\!\!\!\!\! \underset{\text{put a }bomb\text{ in the }sink.}{bmb\ +\  cnc}</math>

The theorem may be written more symmetrically using signed lengths of segments.  That is, take the length {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} to be positive or negative  according to whether {{mvar|A}} is to the left or right of {{mvar|B}} in some fixed orientation of the line. In this formulation, the theorem states that if {{mvar|A, B, C}} are [[collinear]] points, and {{mvar|P}} is any point, then
:<math>\left(\overline{PA}^2\cdot \overline{BC}\right) + \left(\overline{PB}^2\cdot \overline{CA}\right) + \left(\overline{PC}^2\cdot \overline{AB}\right) + \left(\overline{AB}\cdot \overline{BC}\cdot \overline{CA}\right) =0.</math><ref name=Russell>{{harvnb|Russell|1905|loc=p. 3}}</ref>

In the special case where the cevian is a [[median (geometry)|median]] (meaning it divides the opposite side into two segments of equal length), the result is known as [[Apollonius' theorem]].

== Proof ==
The theorem can be proved as an application of the [[law of cosines]].<ref>{{PlanetMath|title=Proof of Stewart's Theorem|urlname=ProofOfStewartsTheorem}}</ref>

Let {{mvar|θ}} be the angle between {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|d}} and {{mvar|θ'}} the [[angle]] between {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|d}}. Then {{mvar|θ'}} is the [[supplementary angle|supplement]] of {{mvar|θ}}, and so {{math|1=cos ''θ' ''= −cos ''θ''}}. Applying the law of cosines in the two small triangles using angles {{mvar|θ}} and {{mvar|θ'}} produces
<math display="block">\begin{align}
c^2 &= m^2 + d^2 - 2dm\cos\theta, \\
b^2  &= n^2 + d^2 - 2dn\cos\theta' \\
&= n^2 + d^2 + 2dn\cos\theta.
\end{align}</math>

Multiplying the first equation by {{mvar|n}} and the third equation by {{mvar|m}} and adding them eliminates {{math|cos ''θ''}}.  One obtains
<math display="block">\begin{align}
b^2m + c^2n &= nm^2 + n^2m + (m+n)d^2 \\
&= (m+n)(mn + d^2) \\
&= a(mn + d^2), \\
\end{align}</math>
which is the required equation.

Alternatively, the theorem can be proved by drawing a perpendicular from the vertex of the triangle to the base and using the [[Pythagorean theorem]] to write the distances {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}}, {{mvar|d}} in terms of the altitude. The left and right hand sides of the equation then reduce algebraically to the same expression.<ref name=Russell />

==History==
According to {{harvtxt|Hutton|Gregory|1843|loc=p. 220}}, Stewart published the result in 1746 when he was a candidate to replace [[Colin Maclaurin]] as Professor of Mathematics at the University of Edinburgh. {{harvtxt|Coxeter|Greitzer|1967|loc=p. 6}} state that the result was probably known to [[Archimedes]] around 300 B.C.E. They go on to say (mistakenly) that the first known proof was provided by R. Simson in 1751. {{harvtxt|Hutton|Gregory|1843}} state that the result is used by Simson in 1748 and by Simpson in 1752, and its first appearance in Europe{{clarification needed|date=October 2024}} given by [[Lazare Carnot]] in 1803.
